question: Can diminishing returns from adding transformer layers be explained by the bias and diversity of layerwise predictions in the residual stream?

key_findings.claim: A squared-error bias-diversity identity makes the ensemble-like benefit of residual-stream modules explicit.
key_findings.evidence: The final residual prediction is decomposed into the average error of module-level predictions minus their dispersion. Lower individual bias and larger disagreement can jointly lower error, but diversity ceases to help without bound because it is coupled to bias and the target.

key_findings.claim: The information-theoretic extension says an added layer helps only insofar as it supplies target-relevant information not redundant with existing layers.
key_findings.evidence: Fano-style error bounds are expressed using mutual information between the target and the set of layer variables. Conditional information gain is submodular under stated conditional-independence or redundancy conditions, yielding diminishing marginal returns as layers accumulate.

key_findings.claim: Empirical layer addition broadly follows diminishing returns, while layer sharing reduces measured diversity and often accuracy.
key_findings.evidence: Across semantic-understanding tasks and several LLM families, intermediate logit-lens-like predictions are used to estimate bias and diversity. MobileLLM layer-shared variants show much lower average diversity than unshared counterparts; the tables also contain task-level exceptions and non-monotonicity, consistent with the theory's conditional-redundancy caveat.

key_findings.claim: The work does not derive parameter scaling laws from training dynamics; it offers an analogy for one depth-related axis.
key_findings.evidence: The theory treats layer outputs as predictor variables and compares their diminishing conditional information with logarithmic-looking empirical curves. It does not predict scaling exponents, compute/data tradeoffs, optimization effects, or width scaling, and the paper explicitly frames diversity as one aspect of parameter scaling.

method.core_idea: Interpret transformer residual additions as a collection of partially redundant predictors and quantify when another layer contributes new target information.
method.mechanism: Project intermediate residual states through the output head, compute layerwise prediction error and diversity, derive information-theoretic error bounds and submodularity conditions, then compare layer-count and layer-sharing trends across language-understanding tasks.
assumptions: Intermediate residual states can be treated as meaningful predictors through the final output head.
Squared-error or classification-information decompositions reflect downstream task performance.
Conditional redundancy behaves sufficiently like the submodular ideal.
Prompted evaluation across the selected LLMs represents general layer-scaling behavior.

techniques.role: Separates individual layer error from complementary disagreement.
Turns intermediate layer states into comparable task predictions.
Defines generalized diversity as new target information conditional on existing layers.
Formalizes diminishing returns under redundancy assumptions.

evaluations.setting: Multiple LLMs on eight semantic-understanding tasks
evaluations.metric: Layerwise accuracy, MSE, bias, and diversity
evaluations.result: Higher performance generally coincides with lower bias and useful diversity, with task-level exceptions
evaluations.baseline: Intermediate versus final layers and different model sizes

evaluations.setting: MobileLLM 125M and 350M with and without recurrent layer sharing
evaluations.result: Layer sharing sharply reduces measured diversity and generally does not improve average accuracy

evaluations.metric: Marginal performance gain per added layer

limitations: Author-stated: probability-based theory and practical logit measurements are not identical.
Author-stated: conditional redundancy can make empirical gains non-monotonic.
Reviewer-identified: the final unembedding may not decode intermediate states faithfully without tuned lenses.
Reviewer-identified: observational diversity does not show that disagreement causes scaling gains.
Reviewer-identified: width, data, compute, and training dynamics—the central variables of scaling-law work—are not modeled.
failure_modes: Intermediate-state projections are miscalibrated, inflating apparent bias.
Layers are diverse in irrelevant directions and add no target information.
Shared layers retain function through recurrent state changes despite low output diversity.
Conditional information is estimated poorly from limited task examples.
A model family changes architecture or training recipe with depth, confounding marginal layer gains.
reusable_insights: Measure target-conditional novelty, not raw representational distance, when assessing layer redundancy.
Separate predictor diversity from predictor quality.
Use layer-sharing and layer-dropping interventions to test observational decompositions.
Avoid calling a diminishing-return analogy a derivation of empirical scaling laws.
open_questions: Can calibrated tuned lenses make bias-diversity measurements invariant to layer basis?
Does actively regularizing conditional layer diversity improve compute-matched performance?
How do attention and MLP modules differ in target-relevant novelty?
Can the framework predict which layers are safely droppable before evaluation?
What changes when width and data scale jointly with depth?

competitive_landscape.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Kaplan et al. fit performance as a function of parameters, data, and compute. This paper does not estimate those exponents; it proposes target-relevant layer diversity as a mechanistic analogy for diminishing returns along depth.

competitive_landscape.title: What Matters in Transformers? Not All Attention is Needed
competitive_landscape.difference: He et al. identify attention components that can be removed or reduced. The present work supplies a bias-diversity and conditional-information lens intended to explain why some added modules have low marginal value.

competitive_landscape.title: Universal Transformers
competitive_landscape.difference: Universal Transformers recurrently reuse a transformation across depth. This paper treats shared-layer MobileLLMs as a diversity-reducing comparison, but does not analyze the recurrent computation mechanisms that can make sharing effective.

competitive_landscape.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
competitive_landscape.difference: Olsson et al. trace a specific circuit that emerges across depth and drives an ability. The current paper is coarser: it summarizes module outputs with bias and diversity rather than identifying causal circuits.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: Layer-output diversity and its submodular target information provide a theoretical link between transformer internals and diminishing parameter-scaling returns.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper derives two decompositions and compares their qualitative predictions with layer-count, model-size, and layer-sharing experiments.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: Bias-diversity and submodular information gain are established tools. Their application to residual-stream layer predictions is a useful diagnostic contribution, but the paper does not explain parameter scaling laws in the usual quantitative sense or establish diversity as causal.

reviewer_notes: Read all 20 pages, including theorems, remaining-problems section, main experiments, MobileLLM table, appendices, and task templates. Four primary arXiv records were checked on 2026-08-23. Claims were narrowed where logit projections, conditional-independence assumptions, and scaling-law terminology exceed the evidence.
